Earlier in 2024, the U.S. Department of Justice filed a lawsuit against Apple, accusing the company of a "smartphone monopoly".

Over the past two years, Apple has publicly expressed opposition to the case on multiple occasions. Now, according to Bloomberg, the Department of Justice and Apple are in settlement discussions over the lawsuit.

Bloomberg noted that Apple has put forward "multiple proposals" so far this year, attempting to reach a settlement with the Department of Justice:

The report also cautioned that, although negotiations are still ongoing, there is no guarantee that Apple and the Department of Justice will ultimately reach an agreement.

The Department of Justice's antitrust lawsuit against Apple centers on five categories of iPhone user experience: super apps, cloud-based streaming games, third-party messaging apps, third-party smartwatches, and third-party digital wallets.

Over the past year, Apple has made substantial changes on issues of concern to the Department of Justice, including adding RCS support in the Messages app, launching a new "Mini App Partner Program" on the App Store, and expanding the openness of iPhone's NFC chip.

Whether these changes will satisfy the Department of Justice remains unknown. Admittedly, political factors are also involved, which Bloomberg also pointed out:

Apple and the Department of Justice recently filed a joint status report with the court, updating the case progress. In addition, Apple earlier this week prevailed in a discovery dispute over obtaining documents from federal government agencies related to the Department of Justice's case.

9to5Mac's view

If Apple and the Department of Justice ultimately reach a settlement, it would significantly lighten the burden on John Ternus, who will take over as Apple's CEO in September.
